summary: Chris Plante's Polygon review praises Super Mario Bros. Wonder as a game that pairs traditional 2D Mario platforming with the surreal, level-warping Wonder Seeds. He credits the badge system, forgiving design and a flood of short-lived ideas for recapturing the inventiveness of the early 2D Mario games. He argues it would be a fitting last big release for the Nintendo Switch, which is expected to be succeeded soon.
one_line: Polygon's review calls Super Mario Bros. Wonder an inventive, generous blend of classic and surreal Mario that suits the Switch's final act.
key_facts: Super Mario Bros. Wonder releases Oct. 20 on Nintendo Switch and was reviewed using a pre-release download code from Nintendo.
Each Wonder stage contains a Wonder Seed that transforms the level, for example by sending gravity into convulsions or turning Mario into creatures or even inanimate objects.
The game spans six worlds, but levels also appear in the hub area and in surprise spots, and bosses show up without warning or are absent in some worlds.
Time limits are gone, and extra lives can be bought cheaply with the game's abundant purple currency.
A new badge system lets players equip one collected badge per stage, with abilities such as a high floating leap, a Piranha Plant grappling hook, and a triple jump tied to a musical rhythm.
Plante used the Safety Bounce badge for later stages with instant-death bottomless pits.
Prince Florian, a little royal bug, wears the badges alongside the player and provides most of the conversation, along with talkative flowers in the Flower Kingdom.
Up to four players can play together; Nabbit and Yoshi take no damage, and the Yoshis keep their tongue attack and floaty jump.
Plante says the game shares the inventiveness of the first four 2D Mario games, the last of which was Super Mario World in 1990.
Wonder uses ideas briefly, such as a sequence of different falling-platform gimmicks, and Plante contrasts this with AAA 'forever games' full of chores and artificial rewards.
Plante says he would be fine if Wonder were the Switch's last big release, with rumors that its successor could arrive early next year.
The original Super Mario Bros. debuted in 1985, and Plante frames the key difference with 2023 as Mario's creators joining in the fun of breaking the machine.
